stories.headline: Eisenkot chosen over Netanyahu to form Israel’s next government
stories.summary: Israel's president asked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next gov't over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

sources.title: Al Jazeera: Eisenkot chosen over Netanyahu to form Israel’s next government
BBC News: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
NPR: Israeli president invites Netanyahu's opposition leader to broker new government
The Hill: Israeli president picks Netanyahu's rival Eisenkot to form new government

stories.now: BBC News: Neither PM Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor that of his rival secured a majority in last week's election. NPR: Israel's political landscape shifts as President Herzog hands opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government, dealing a blow to Benjamin Netanyahu's grip on power.
stories.backstory: Israel voted on Oct. 27 and neither Netanyahu's coalition nor Eisenkot's bloc reached a governing majority. Eisenkot, a former army chief, said he would not sit in a government led by Netanyahu. Herzog had until Nov. 11 to pick a candidate and said he would weigh each side's ability to form a coalition, not just the count of recommendations. If no one succeeds, Israel faces another election.

stories.headline: Meet Stephen Miller, Trump's new chief of staff: 5 things to know
stories.summary: President Trump announced Friday that longtime White House aide Stephen Miller would be his next chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles — who has served in the role since Trump returned to office. Miller is an immigration hardliner and Trump loyalist who has been with the president since he launched his first campaign.

stories.backstory: Wiles ran Trump's 2024 campaign and was named chief of staff after his election win, the first woman in the role. Miller worked in Trump's first-term White House and returned in 2025 as a senior policy adviser focused on immigration and deportations. Republicans lost the House and likely the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, prompting questions about how the White House would respond.
